text:
## Observations

1. If \(K\) pairs are possible in \([L,R]\), the \(K\) smallest mochi and the \(K\) largest mochi in that interval can be paired in sorted order.
2. For a top at index \(i\), the valid bottoms start at the first index \(p_i\) with \(A_{p_i}\ge 2A_i\). These first valid indices are nondecreasing as \(i\) increases.
3. For a positive \(K\) with \(2K\le R-L+1\), the sorted pairing is feasible exactly when the maximum of \(p_i-i\) over \(L\le i\le L+K-1\) is at most \(R-K+1-L\).
4. Zero pairs are always feasible, and discarding pairs from any feasible arrangement gives a feasible arrangement with fewer pairs.

## Solution sketch

> If \(K\) pairs are possible in \([L,R]\), the \(K\) smallest mochi and the \(K\) largest mochi in that interval can be paired in sorted order.

1. To justify the pairing, sort the tops and bottoms of any feasible arrangement separately. The \(j\) smallest bottoms had \(j\) distinct tops, each at most half the size of the \(j\)-th smallest bottom. Thus the \(j\)-th smallest top fits on that bottom. Replacing the sorted tops with the interval’s \(K\) smallest mochi can only decrease their sizes, and replacing the sorted bottoms with its \(K\) largest can only increase theirs. The two groups are disjoint because \(2K\le R-L+1\).

> For a top at index \(i\), the valid bottoms start at the first index \(p_i\) with \(A_{p_i}\ge 2A_i\). These first valid indices are nondecreasing as \(i\) increases.

2. Compute all \(p_i\) in one pass with a forward-only pointer. For each \(i\), advance the pointer past sizes strictly below \(2A_i\). This accepts equality and handles repeated sizes. Use \(N+1\) when the pointer runs past the array, and store \(p_i-i\) for each index. The pass takes \(O(N)\) time.

> For a positive \(K\) with \(2K\le R-L+1\), the sorted pairing is feasible exactly when the maximum of \(p_i-i\) over \(L\le i\le L+K-1\) is at most \(R-K+1-L\).

3. In the sorted pairing, the bottom for top \(i\) is at index \(i+(R-K+1-L)\). Every bottom must reach its top’s threshold \(p_i\), which gives the range-maximum test. A sentinel of \(N+1\) makes the test fail whenever that top has no valid bottom. Build a sparse table on the stored differences, starting with blocks of length one and combining adjacent half-blocks for each larger power of two. For a test interval, take the maximum of the two blocks of the largest power-of-two length that fits, one aligned to each end. The blocks cover the interval, and overlap is harmless when taking a maximum. This gives \(O(1)\) feasibility tests after \(O(N\log N)\) preprocessing time and space.

> Zero pairs are always feasible, and discarding pairs from any feasible arrangement gives a feasible arrangement with fewer pairs.

4. For each query, binary search for the largest feasible \(K\) from \(0\) through \(\lfloor(R-L+1)/2\rfloor\). Use \(0\) as the known feasible lower bound and one above the upper limit as the known infeasible bound, so every tested candidate is positive and within the size limit. The search returns \(0\) if no pair fits and reaches the upper limit if all possible pairs fit. Print each result on its own line in query order. The total running time is \(O(N\log N+Q\log N)\), with \(O(N\log N)\) auxiliary space when processing queries one at a time.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
